messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Sunit has been a graphic designer for over fifteen years, working from his home office in a quiet suburban neighborhood. His life took a sudden and devastating turn when he witnessed an incident involving police that left him deeply traumatized. Sunit’s trauma began on the day he was walking back home after a late meeting with a client and saw a heated confrontation between the police and a man he knew from his community. The man, someone he trusted, was in handcuffs, bleeding from a wound on his head. The scene was chaotic, with sirens blaring and officers shouting commands. Sunit tried to intervene but was forced back by the police, who were convinced he was a threat due to his attire resembling that of the suspect’s allies. Since then, certain smells and sights have triggered vivid recollections of this traumatic event. The burnt smell of the burning tires nearby on that fateful day immediately transports him back to the scene, replaying those harrowing moments over and over again in his mind. Every time he sees someone in a uniform, especially police officers, it brings back intense feelings of guilt and betrayal. When Sunit tries to make sense of what happened, he finds himself struggling with words. He knows what transpired but cannot articulate the sequence of events clearly. When he attempts to explain the encounter, his thoughts get jumbled, and he loses the thread of his narrative mid-sentence. This inability to recount the incident clearly exacerbates his feelings of guilt and mistrust. Sunit has come to believe that the world is a dangerous place where people cannot be trusted, especially those in authority. He feels betrayed by someone who was once close to him and now views every uniformed figure as a potential threat. These beliefs have led him to adopt several maladaptive strategies. Before any interaction, he meticulously rehearses what he will say, convinced that his words might incriminate or endanger him. This hypervigilance extends beyond mere thoughts; Sunit actively avoids making future plans, fearing they could be disrupted by unexpected encounters with authority figures. His mistrust has also infiltrated his professional life as a graphic designer. He often rehearses conversations with clients and colleagues, worrying about saying the wrong thing or being misunderstood. These strategies have created a reinforcing cycle of negative appraisals and triggers. The more he avoids future plans and remains vigilant for dangerous people, the stronger his feelings of mistrust and danger become. Each time he encounters an authority figure in uniform or smells something reminiscent of that day, it intensifies his memory difficulties and guilt. Sunit’s avoidance has strained his relationships with colleagues who find him distant and preoccupied. He feels increasingly isolated, unable to share his experiences due to his fear of being misunderstood or judged. The weight of these symptoms finally compelled Sunit to seek help after a particularly distressing encounter at the supermarket where he broke down in tears upon seeing a police officer. Sunit is most afraid that his fears will overwhelm him and that he won’t be able to maintain his professional life or relationships. He hopes for understanding and support, believing that with help, he might find the words to explain what happened and regain some sense of trust and safety in the world around him.
